analysis.title: A hiccup or the start of a mega correction? (Across the Americas)
key_insights: Initial jobless claims fell from a revised 200K to 194K in the week ended October 17, a four-year low. Continuing claims rose from 1,703K to 1,728K in the week ended October 10, which Natixis reads as a continuing low-hire, low-fire labor market.

Natixis expects the FOMC to leave the policy rate unchanged next week, with the upper bound staying at 4.00%. The September core CPI was hotter than expected but not far enough off expectations to make a hike likely in October.

Fed communication supports a pause. Vice Chair Jefferson wants more time to assess data, NY Fed's Williams saw no urgency to act in October, Waller stressed flexibility on timing, and Chair Warsh did not push back on market expectations of a pause at the IMF meetings. Natixis also thinks political scrutiny ahead of the midterms argues against a hike.

Brent crude closed at its highest level since early May on renewed Middle East tensions and reports that President Trump is preparing to resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections. A sustained rise in energy prices could slow the disinflation seen in the latest PCE prints.

Next week's calendar includes Conference Board Consumer Confidence on Tuesday and September PCE on Thursday. Both headline and core PCE are expected to run hotter than the prior month, and more than half of the CPI items that rose month on month were energy related.

Treasuries moved from driving the global rates selloff to following external factors this week: oil swings, AI optimism and worries, and French OAT underperformance late in the week. Bund moves influenced Treasuries more than anything else over the past two weeks.

The correlation of bunds to Treasuries over the past two weeks is 0.88, down from 0.96 in September and the 0.94 full-year figure. Futures positioning showed net buying across nearly the whole complex, with OATs the notable exception.

TIC data through August showed foreign official holdings of marketable Treasury debt down 0.2 points to 11.8%, while foreign private holdings rose 0.1 points to 17.5%. Japan's holdings fell $35.6bn, Canada rose $38bn and France rose $15bn. The Fed's custody holdings rose $18.5bn last week but are down $42bn over the last month and $169bn year to date.
Foreign participation in the October 10yr and 30yr auctions was strong at 21% and 25%, against pre-September year-to-date averages of 17% and 13%.

Natixis stays long 10s on the 5s10s30s swap fly. The fly has performed as yields fell, but 1m10y vol has not dropped as much as expected and the fly is cheaper than fair value by less than before. Natixis holds the position because it expects vol to fall as rates settle into a higher range for the next few weeks.

Natixis remains long 2yr notes from 4.88% with a 4.42% target. It would tactically unwind if cumulative Fed pricing for the next 12 months falls to 50bps, which it sees as a near-term floor. The position earns about 13bps of carry and roll over three months.

Natixis favors steepeners but remains cautious. A slowdown in AI investment could let the long end outperform, and the 2s10s weekly chart showed a long-legged doji suggesting a near-term top in the flattening. Natixis would rather wait for entry in the low- to mid-20s than enter the steepener now.

Brazil's presidential run-off is Sunday October 25. Polls narrowed from about 5 points to about 2 points in favor of Flavio Bolsonaro. Natixis sees part of this as mean reversion toward his 1.87% first-round margin and still considers him the favorite.

Natixis argues Brazilian voters will pick the candidate they dislike less. PoderData shows 48% would never vote for Lula versus 44% for Bolsonaro, and Datafolha shows unaligned voters at 59% Bolsonaro and 41% Lula.

In Natixis's pre-election survey, 76% of respondents named fiscal responsibility as the main concern under a Lula win, and 83% expect USD/BRL above 5.30 by end of October in that case, with an interpolated median of 5.39.

Under a Flavio Bolsonaro win, the top concerns were delivering fiscal adjustment (67%), efforts to free Jair Bolsonaro (40%) and frictions with the Supreme Court (33%). The survey's interpolated median for USD/BRL by end of October is 4.87 in that case.

Banxico's October 8 minutes showed at least three board members open to discussing a cut, but nobody voted for one. After upside inflation surprises and MXN depreciation, Natixis sees the chances of a cut as slim.

Mexico H1 October headline inflation was 0.41% 2w/2w against 0.38% expected, and core was 0.25% against 0.17% expected. Core is 3.78% y/y, and non-core inflation is now above 3.0% y/y, up from about 1% a couple of months ago.
